points.title: Transmission medium: wired and wireless
points.must: Definition of transmission medium; wired (guided: copper, fibre) vs wireless (unguided: radio, microwave, infrared).
points.model: Transmission medium = the physical path along which data signals travel between devices. Wired (guided) media: copper cable (electrical signals), fibre-optic cable (light). Wireless (unguided) media: radio waves, microwaves, infrared through the air.

points.title: Bandwidth, latency, interference, attenuation
points.must: Definitions of bandwidth (data per second, bit/s), latency (delay), interference (unwanted signals corrupting data → re-sending), attenuation (signal weakens with distance).
points.model: Bandwidth = maximum amount of data sent per second (bit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s). Latency = delay before data arrives (e.g. satellite ~0.5 s). Interference = unwanted signals (motors, microwaves, other Wi-Fi) that corrupt data, so it must be re-sent. Attenuation = weakening of the signal over distance.

points.title: Twisted-pair cable
points.must: Four twisted copper pairs, electrical signals; twisting cancels noise; UTP vs STP; Cat5e/Cat6; RJ45; about 100 m; cheap; used from computers to switches.
points.model: Twisted pair (Ethernet cable): 8 copper wires in 4 twisted pairs, electrical signals; twisting cancels most outside noise. UTP = unshielded, cheap, flexible; STP = shielded with foil, for noisy places (factories). Cat5e 1 Gbit/s, Cat6 up to 10 Gbit/s. RJ45 plug. Max about 100 m per run. Used to connect computers to switches.

points.title: Coaxial cable
points.must: Copper core, insulation, metal shield, jacket; well shielded; used for cable TV/satellite/old LANs; thicker and slower than fibre.
points.model: Coaxial: one copper core, insulation, woven metal shield, outer jacket. Shield gives good protection from interference. Used for cable TV, satellite dishes, old bus LANs. Thicker, stiffer, replaced in LANs by twisted pair and fibre.

points.title: Fibre-optic cable
points.must: Pulses of light in glass; total internal reflection; multi-mode vs single-mode; advantages (bandwidth, distance, no EMI, hard to tap, light) and disadvantages (cost, fragile, special joining).
points.model: Fibre-optic: data sent as pulses of light (on = 1, off = 0) through thin glass fibres; light stays in the core by total internal reflection. Multi-mode: wider core, cheaper, up to a few hundred m. Single-mode: narrow core, tens of km, WAN/undersea cables. + very high bandwidth, very long distances, not affected by electrical interference, very hard to tap, thin and light. − expensive cable and equipment, fragile, needs special tools to join.

points.title: Wireless and Wi-Fi access points
points.must: Wireless = electromagnetic waves through air; definition of wireless access point; SSID; range about 30–50 m indoors, weakened by walls; bandwidth shared between devices.
points.model: Wireless = data sent through the air as electromagnetic waves (mostly radio). Wireless access point = device that connects wireless devices to a wired network. SSID = the network's name. One AP covers about 30–50 m indoors; walls, metal and distance weaken the signal. All devices on one AP share its bandwidth, so more users → less speed each.

points.title: 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz
points.must: 2.4 GHz: longer range, through walls, slower, crowded/more interference; 5 GHz: faster, more channels, less interference, shorter range.
points.model: 2.4 GHz: longer range, passes walls better, but slower and crowded (shared with Bluetooth, microwave ovens) → more interference. 5 GHz: faster, more channels, less interference, but shorter range and weakened more by walls → more access points needed.

points.title: Wireless security
points.must: Why needed (signal can be intercepted outside); encryption definition; WPA2/WPA3 (not WEP); strong passwords/user accounts; guest network; change default passwords.
points.model: Radio signals pass through walls, so anyone in range can try to intercept data or join. Encryption = scrambling data with a key so an interceptor cannot understand it. Use WPA2 or WPA3 (not WEP), strong passwords or user accounts, a separate guest network for visitors, change the router's default admin password, update firmware.

points.title: Other wireless technologies
points.must: Bluetooth (~10 m, PAN, low power), mobile 4G/5G (masts, km, data plan), satellite (anywhere, high latency), microwave (line of sight between buildings), infrared (few m, line of sight).
points.model: Bluetooth: ~10 m, low power, PAN (headphones, smartwatch). 4G/5G: radio to masts, km range, on the move, pay for data. Satellite: almost anywhere (ships, remote areas), high latency, affected by weather. Microwave link: dish to dish, km, needs line of sight. Infrared: few metres, line of sight, TV remotes.

points.title: Speed, reliability and interference compared
points.must: Wired faster and constant (dedicated link, protected signal) whereas wireless slower, varies with distance/walls/users, more interference and re-sending.
points.model: Wired is faster and constant because each cable is a dedicated link and the signal is protected, whereas wireless bandwidth is shared and falls with distance, walls and the number of users. Wired has little interference (fibre none), whereas wireless suffers from other networks, microwaves and walls, so data is re-sent and connections drop.

points.title: Security, mobility, cost compared
points.must: Wired more secure (physical access needed) vs wireless interceptable (needs WPA2/3); wireless gives mobility and connects socket-less devices; wired costly/disruptive to install, wireless cheap and quick to add devices.
points.model: Security: wired needs physical access to tap, whereas wireless signals can be intercepted from outside → needs encryption. Mobility: wireless users move freely and phones/tablets without sockets can connect, whereas wired devices are fixed to a socket. Cost: laying cable is expensive and disruptive (drilling walls, re-cabling to move), whereas wireless is cheaper and quicker — a few APs and devices just join.

points.title: Range, number of devices, safety
points.must: Copper ~100 m, fibre km vs AP 30–50 m; switch ports limit wired devices vs many wireless devices sharing bandwidth; cables are a trip hazard.
points.model: Range: copper run ~100 m, fibre km, whereas one AP ~30–50 m. Devices: wired limited by switch ports (24/48), wireless accepts many but each gets less bandwidth. Safety: cables on the floor are a trip hazard / fire risk if damaged; wireless has no cables.

points.title: Combined networks and backbone
points.must: Definition of backbone; organisations use wired backbone/servers/desktops plus wireless for mobile devices; APs are cabled to the wired network.
points.model: Backbone = the main high-capacity part of a network connecting switches, buildings and servers; normally wired, often fibre. Most organisations combine: wired for backbone, servers, desktops, printers and the APs; wireless for laptops, tablets, phones and visitors. Data goes wirelessly only for the last few metres to the AP.

points.title: Worked example: choosing connections
points.must: A scenario decision with reasons, e.g. clinic: server and reception wired (confidential records, reliable), staff Wi-Fi with WPA3, separate guest Wi-Fi for patients' phones.
points.model: Clinic: server + reception PCs wired — medical records are confidential (cannot be intercepted) and need a fast constant link; doctors' PCs wired for large X-ray files, plus staff Wi-Fi with WPA3 for tablets; waiting room: separate guest Wi-Fi because patients' phones have no socket and must not reach the records. Steps: devices move? data size? security? building? cost/time? → choose and justify.
